title: African cities, American-style music and coconut drying
summary: They toured all over Africa; the cities were modern, local bands tried to play American music while tribal drumming was separate, and he saw green coconuts laid out in the sun beside ships waiting to load.

story.theme_name: Going abroad: American jazz musicians touring and living in Europe
story.community_name: Going abroad: touring Europe and Japan

blocks.x: So you went to Ghana and the Cameroons. Did you go anywhere else in Africa?
Yeah, we went all over Africa. Abidjan [Kenya, Ivory Coast, Ghana] and all them places. I can't think of all them funny names.
Did the life differ very much from one country to another in Africa?

In Africa? No. Well, the only thing, the cities. But you'd be surprised. They got big cities and modern. And they're washed, they're clean, but they're funky. They're clean but they're really -- they wash. You can see them all along the road wash-bathing, but you get in an airplane with them and look out, you can cut that funk with a knife. But outside of that --
How about the music? What kind of music did you hear in Africa?
They're trying to play our music. That's all they do, playing our music. That other business with the tom-tom, that's tribal business. That's tribal music.
Was there any effort to combine them, their own tribal kinds of rhythms with American jazz?
If they want to, with the tom-toms --
not -- what do you call them things? Tom-toms, like bongos. But they got the good rhythm, though. They are fantastic. And you see how they do the coconut. That's the first time I've ever seen that.

They're green and they got like a huge table and netting and it's on the side of the road. And they take all these green coconuts and lay them out there and the sun, the sun is what turns them brown. That's when they begin to get cocoa.
Then you see all these ships waiting to be loaded to go to different countries. It's fantastic.
